reasoning_traces.think:
Expected goals (xG) represent a probabilistic model of goal-scoring likelihood, grounded in shot features like position and angle. The sigmoidal transformation of linear combinations of these features yields a bounded probability estimate. Gradient boosting aggregates weak learners to iteratively refine predictions, capturing non-linear dependencies in event data. These models are trained on structured inputs such as shot coordinates and angles, producing scalar outputs representing expected goals. The derived action-value function allows GSE to simulate player behavior and assess tactical efficacy. Dualities emerge in how xG reflects both objective shot quality and subjective team performance. Failure modes include overfitting due to insufficient data or misalignment of training and test distributions. The model assumes independence of shot features and ignores dynamic context like defensive pressure. Historical lineage traces back to early statistical models of football, evolving with machine learning. Opposing agents—teams—optimize their strategies against xG-based expectations, creating adversarial feedback loops. Anti-collinearity ensures that features like distance and angle contribute independently to prediction accuracy.
